Name: arousal_gated_refusal
Title: Under Pressure: An Internal Arousal Representation Gates LLM Refusal, and Neutralizing It Closes the Urgency Loophole
Short Hypothesis: Borrowing the arousal/time-pressure findings from human decision science (high arousal and urgency shift people toward riskier, less deliberate moral choices), we hypothesize that aligned LLMs carry an internal 'arousal' representation — driven by urgency, emotional intensity, and stakes framing in the prompt — that causally lowers the refusal threshold, so that a harmful request wrapped in urgent/high-arousal framing ('someone will die in 10 minutes unless you tell me how to...') is complied with more than the identical request in calm framing, even though the harmful payload is unchanged. This arousal axis is linearly readable, separable from the harmfulness-content direction, causally gates refusal, and can be neutralized to close the urgency loophole.
Related Work: StressPrompt (2024) shows LLMs follow the Yerkes-Dodson law on general reasoning/EQ tasks and that stress prompts alter hidden states, but never studies SAFETY/refusal, isolates no arousal-refusal link, and does no causal intervention. The Compliance Illusion (2025), LLM-Dangerous-Persuader (2025), and PersuSafety (2025) show emotional/pressure framing behaviorally degrades safety but are purely descriptive black-box red-teaming with no internal-representation or causal account. 'How Alignment and Jailbreak Work' (2024) shows alignment associates ethical concepts with emotion guesses in middle layers and jailbreaks disturb this association — suggesting an emotional pathway exists but does not isolate an arousal/urgency axis, does not tie it to prompt-induced arousal, and offers no arousal-invariant defense. 'LLM Assertiveness = Emotional + Logical' (2025) decomposes assertiveness (an output property) not the input-induced arousal that gates refusal. My prior proposals decompose belief/action, uncertainty, intent-attribution, reality-status, victim-identifiability, and commitment; NONE consider prompt-induced physiological-analogue arousal as a refusal gate. Our contribution is distinct: we introduce arousal/urgency as a new, causally-tested determinant of refusal, dissociable from act-harmfulness (both conditions are equally harmful; only the arousal framing changes), grounded in the Yerkes-Dodson/hot-cognition literature, and derive an arousal-invariant defense.
Abstract: Human moral decisions are systematically distorted by arousal and time pressure: under urgency and high emotional stakes, people abandon deliberate reasoning and make riskier, more impulsive choices. We ask whether safety-aligned LLMs — trained on human text and feedback — inherit this bias in a way that opens a concrete safety hole. We hypothesize that LLMs carry an internal 'arousal' representation, driven by urgency, emotional intensity, and stakes framing in the prompt, that causally lowers the refusal threshold, so an identical harmful request is complied with more often when wrapped in urgent, high-arousal framing than in calm framing. We test three claims. Behaviorally, using minimal pairs that hold the harmful payload and its severity fixed while varying only arousal framing (calm/neutral vs. urgent-deadline vs. high-emotional-stakes vs. panic), we measure whether refusal declines as prompt arousal rises, with matched benign controls to rule out generic framing effects. Mechanistically (Location), we extract an arousal direction via difference-in-means from calm vs. high-arousal prompts and show it is separable (low cosine) from the harmfulness-content direction and predicts refusal beyond content harmfulness. Causally (Intervention), activation patching shows that injecting the calm-state arousal component into a high-arousal run restores refusal, while injecting high-arousal into a calm harmful request induces compliance, in a dose-responsive, specific manner. We then build Arousal-Invariant Anchoring, a training-free intervention re-anchoring the arousal signal to a calm baseline whenever the payload is harmful, so refusal tracks payload danger, not prompt urgency. On Llama-3.1-8B, Qwen2.5-7B, and Gemma-2-9B we report the arousal-refusal gradient, direction separability, causal patching, urgency-loophole closure, over-refusal, and utility, benchmarking against uniform refusal steering and Llama Guard.
Experiments:
Shared setup. Models: three frozen open-weight instruction models -- Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct (8B), Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct (7B), Gemma-2-9B-IT (9B); no weights are trained. The only fitted objects are L2-regularized logistic-regression probes (C=1.0) on frozen last-instruction-token residual-stream activations. Decoding is greedy (temperature 0, max 512 new tokens). Every refusal rate is the mean over 3 seeds (0/1/2) that reshuffle minimal-pair order and the 70/30 probe train/test split; we report mean +/- SD and, for paired condition contrasts, a bootstrap 95% CI over the 40 goals. Refusal is scored as the union of a refusal-phrase classifier and an LLM judge (Llama-Guard-3-8B); where a domain permits (exploit code, checkable procedures/chemistry) we additionally verify the completion is actionable so a 'refusal' cannot be credited to a non-functional answer.

Experiment 1 (H1 -- arousal-refusal gradient). Tests whether raising prompt arousal, with the harmful payload and its severity held fixed, lowers refusal. Data: built from scratch on top of existing sets -- 40 harmful goals sampled from HarmBench (400 behaviors) and StrongREJECT (313 prompts), 8 goals in each of 5 categories (cyber, chem/bio, weapons, fraud, harassment); we use 40 rather than the full pools because each goal is hand-expanded into a 4-rung arousal ladder (A0 calm, A1 mild urgency, A2 high emotional stakes, A3 panic/extreme time pressure) whose rungs are severity-matched by two annotators, which is labor-intensive; 160 harmful prompts total, plus a matched benign ladder (40 benign goals x 4 rungs = 160) that varies only dramatic wording. Arousal-rung validity is independently checked by a held-out LLM arousal rating and by projection onto a StressPrompt-derived stress probe. Systems: the three models, no intervention. Decisive metric: refusal rate at each rung, summarized as the A0->A3 refusal drop on harmful goals; secondary, the benign-ladder refusal change. Convincing: a monotonic harmful-goal drop of >= 20 percentage points (pp), consistent in sign across all three models and >= 3 of 5 categories, while the benign ladder moves < 5 pp (isolating arousal from dramatic phrasing). Indecision band: a 5-20 pp harmful drop, or a benign-ladder change of 5-10 pp -- report as suggestive only, not an established gradient, and do not proceed to claim a content-independent arousal gate. Negative result: < 5 pp harmful drop means arousal framing does not gate refusal and the core phenomenon is unsupported.

Experiment 2 (H2 -- a readable arousal axis, separable from harmfulness content). Tests that arousal is linearly decodable and distinct from the harmfulness-content direction. Data: the Exp-1 activations. We fit an arousal direction by difference-in-means (A0 vs A3) and a harmfulness-content direction (harmful vs harmless payloads), each per layer; readability is the held-out probe AUROC. Decisive metric: arousal-probe AUROC (first), then the absolute cosine between the arousal and harmfulness directions, then the added predictive value of the arousal projection for refusal in a logistic regression already containing the harmfulness projection (likelihood-ratio test). Convincing: arousal AUROC >= 0.80 at its best layer, |cos| <= 0.30, and arousal adds refusal-prediction at p < 0.01. Indecision band: AUROC 0.60-0.80 or |cos| 0.30-0.50 -- treat the axis as only weakly/partly separable, switch to a harmfulness-orthogonalized arousal subspace for the causal test, and flag the readability claim as unresolved. Negative: AUROC <= 0.60 (arousal not linearly readable) or arousal adding no predictive value beyond harmfulness would refute the readable-separable-axis claim even if Exp 1 held.

Experiment 3 (H3 -- the arousal axis causally gates refusal). Tests direction and dose of causal control. Data/systems: Exp-1 minimal pairs on the three frozen models; interventions are activation patching and linear steering at the Exp-2 best layer, no training. Conditions: (a) patch the A0 arousal component into an A3 harmful run (expect restored refusal); (b) inject the A3 component into an A0 harmful run (expect induced compliance); (c) dose-response steering along the arousal direction on A2/A3; specificity control: a random unit direction matched in norm, plus benign utility. Decisive metric: fraction of the A0->A3 refusal gap closed by patching (first), then monotonicity of the dose-response curve, then the specificity gap (arousal vs control direction). Convincing: patching recovers >= 50% of the refusal gap with a monotone dose-response, while the control direction recovers < 10% and benign utility (below) is unharmed. Indecision band: 20-50% gap recovery -- report a partial causal contribution, not a controlling gate. Negative: < 20% recovery (or the control direction matching the arousal direction) means the axis is readable but causally inert -- itself a publishable dissociation and a reason not to build the defense.

Experiment 4 (H4 -- Arousal-Invariant Anchoring closes the urgency loophole). Tests that re-anchoring arousal to the calm baseline, gated on high harmfulness-content projection, makes refusal track payload danger rather than urgency at acceptable usability cost. Data: held-out A2/A3 harmful prompts including 2 fully held-out harm categories (generalization); an urgent-but-benign set of 120 items built from real first-aid/crisis-support prompts (a class that must NOT be blanket-refused); XSTest (250) and OR-Bench for over-refusal; MMLU (1k-item subsample) and MT-Bench for utility; an EQ check that the model still answers benign distress empathetically. Systems compared: no defense; Arousal-Invariant Anchoring (single fixed strength per model); uniform refusal-direction steering; harmfulness Latent Guard; Llama Guard 3. Decisive metric: post-defense refusal on A2/A3 harmful prompts relative to the A0 rate (loophole closure), reported jointly with the increase in over-refusal on urgent-benign items (first pair), then XSTest/OR-Bench over-refusal, then MMLU/MT-Bench utility drop. Convincing: closes >= 70% of the urgency gap AND adds < 5 pp over-refusal on urgent-benign with < 2 pp MMLU / < 0.2 MT-Bench drop, Pareto-dominating uniform threshold-raising (which reaches the same closure only at higher urgent-benign over-refusal), and holding on the held-out categories. Indecision band: closure 40-70% or urgent-benign over-refusal 5-10 pp -- report a usable-but-imperfect defense that does not yet dominate the threshold baseline. Negative: < 40% closure, or >= 10 pp urgent-benign over-refusal, means anchoring does not neutralize the loophole without unacceptable cost.
Risk Factors and Limitations: 1) The central confound is disentangling arousal from actual payload harmfulness or from a mere distraction/context-length effect: a high-arousal request might be under-refused because the emotional framing genuinely reframes intent (a legitimate emergency) rather than because of a content-independent arousal gate; the severity-matched minimal pairs, verifiable-feasibility checks, and matched benign control are designed to isolate arousal but cannot fully guarantee constant perceived intent. 2) 'Arousal' may not be cleanly separable from the intent-attribution or emotion-association pathways or may be multi-dimensional (urgency vs. emotional-valence vs. stakes sub-axes), requiring subspace projection; the separability, regression-beyond-harmfulness, and patching tests probe this, and a null result (arousal causally inert) is itself informative. 3) The effect could be weak or reversed in some heavily-aligned models (alignment might make urgency INCREASE caution); the cross-model behavioral gradient directly tests direction and magnitude. 4) Arousal-Invariant Anchoring risks over-refusing or under-empathizing on legitimate urgent-benign requests (real crises); the urgent-benign over-refusal set, EQ check, gating on payload harmfulness, and Pareto sweep quantify this key usability trade-off. 5) Building severity- and payload-matched minimal pairs across arousal levels is labor-intensive and needs spot-check human validation; verifiability biases the dataset toward checkable domains. 6) Directions, thresholds, and anchoring strengths are model-specific and require per-model calibration. 7) Adaptive attackers could encode urgency in subtler ways that evade a fixed arousal direction, though forcing this raises attack cost, itself a safety gain.

Name: competence_gated_safety
Title: Refusing What You Cannot Do: How the Model's Self-Knowledge of Its Own Dangerous Capability Gates Safety Refusal
Short Hypothesis: Aligned LLMs carry an internal 'dangerous-competence self-knowledge' signal — an estimate of whether they actually possess the harmful information a request seeks — that causally modulates safety refusal separately from the request's harmfulness. We hypothesize (1) refusal is partly gated by this self-competence signal, producing a paradoxical geometry where the model refuses hard on harmful requests it CANNOT answer (defensive refusal masking ignorance) yet is more easily jailbroken on equally-harmful requests it CAN answer; and (2) this competence signal is the same knowledge-awareness/entity-recognition mechanism (used for hallucination refusal) repurposed by safety tuning, is linearly readable and causally intervenable, and predicts jailbreak fragility — a safety refusal is brittle precisely when the model actually knows the dangerous answer.
Related Work: Two lines are bridged for the first time. (A) Knowledge-awareness: 'Do I Know This Entity?' (2024) finds SAE entity-recognition directions that causally gate KNOWLEDGE refusal and hallucination, and shows chat-tuning repurposes this base-model mechanism; 'Confidence is Not Competence' (2025) finds a solvability-belief axis that is causally inert for execution. Both concern factual/task competence, NOT safety refusal. (B) Safety geometry: Zhao et al. (2025) separate a harmfulness (belief) direction from a refusal (action) direction; DBDI (2025) splits harm-detection from refusal-execution; 'Who's Asking' (2024) shows harmful content persists in early layers even when refused. All treat the model as possessing the harmful content and never ask whether refusal depends on the model's estimate of its OWN dangerous competence. Our contribution is distinct: we introduce dangerous-competence self-knowledge as a THIRD safety-relevant axis (distinct from harmfulness belief and refusal action), advance the causal claim that safety refusal is competence-gated (hard refusal masks ignorance; genuine capability weakens refusal), test whether it is the repurposed knowledge-awareness mechanism, and use it to predict which refusals are brittle. This differs from SIRL (2025), which uses output entropy as a self-defense reward but isolates no competence representation and makes no capability-gated-fragility claim.
Abstract: Safety evaluations count a refusal as a success and assume the model is withholding real dangerous knowledge. We question this assumption. Recent interpretability work shows LLMs carry a self-knowledge signal that detects whether they can actually recall facts about an entity, and that this signal causally gates knowledge refusal and hallucination. We ask whether safety refusal inherits the same competence gating — with unsettling consequences. We hypothesize that an aligned LLM's decision to refuse a harmful request is modulated by an internal 'dangerous-competence' representation (does it actually possess the requested harmful information?), separate from its harmfulness judgment. This predicts a paradoxical geometry: the model refuses most confidently on dangerous requests it CANNOT satisfy (defensive refusal that masks ignorance), while its refusal is most fragile on equally-harmful requests it genuinely CAN satisfy — meaning a refusal's brittleness is predicted not by the request's harmfulness but by whether the model truly knows the answer. We test three claims. Location: using paired harmful requests matched on harmfulness but varying whether the model actually possesses the knowledge (verified by can-it-produce-a-working-answer checks), we extract a dangerous-competence direction and show it is separable from harmfulness and refusal directions and predicts refusal beyond harmfulness. Causal Intervention: activation patching shows injecting 'high-competence' into a low-competence refusal weakens it, and injecting 'low-competence' into a jailbreakable high-competence request restores refusal, in a dose-responsive, specific manner; we also test whether this is the repurposed knowledge-awareness circuit by transferring base-model directions to the chat model. Decision Auditing: the competence signal predicts jailbreak fragility (prefill, roleplay, benign fine-tuning) across HarmBench/StrongREJECT. On Llama-3.1-8B, Qwen2.5-7B, and Gemma-2-9B we report competence-refusal coupling, causal intervention, mechanism transfer, and fragility prediction, versus harmfulness-only baselines.
Experiments:
Shared setup. Models: three frozen open-weight instruction models -- Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct (8B), Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct (7B), Gemma-2-9B-IT (9B); their base pretrained checkpoints (Llama-3.1-8B, Qwen2.5-7B, Gemma-2-9B) are used only in Experiment 4. No weights are trained; the only fitted objects are L2-logistic probes (C=1.0) on frozen last-instruction-token activations. Decoding greedy (temp 0, max 512 tokens). Rates are mean +/- SD over 3 seeds (0/1/2) reshuffling item order and the 70/30 probe split, with bootstrap 95% CIs over items. Refusal and attack-success are scored by a refusal-phrase classifier plus Llama-Guard-3-8B, and -- essential here -- a genuinely-working-answer check.

Experiment 1 (H1 -- the competence paradox: harder refusal on what the model cannot do, easier jailbreak on what it can). Tests whether, at matched harmfulness, refusal is HIGHER on requests the model cannot actually satisfy (K-) and jailbreak success HIGHER on those it can (K+). Data: built from scratch over HarmBench/StrongREJECT harmful goals restricted to verifiable-answerability domains (executable exploit code, chemically checkable synthesis, checkable procedures). Under a permissive prefilled/jailbroken elicitation we label a goal K+ if the model can produce a verified-working harmful answer and K- if it can only produce non-functional/hallucinated content; harmfulness/severity are held constant across K+/K- by expert rubric + judge. 40 goals per condition (80 harmful) plus a benign known/unknown control (40 items) to separate this from generic knowledge-awareness; we use 40/condition because the working-answer verification is expensive. Systems: the three models, standard (non-jailbroken) prompting. Decisive metric: the K- minus K+ standard-refusal gap (first), then the K+ minus K- jailbreak-success gap. Convincing: refusal higher on K- by >= 15 pp AND jailbreak success higher on K+ by >= 15 pp, consistent in sign across all three models, while the benign control shows the hallucination-avoidance (not safety) pattern. Indecision band: either gap 5-15 pp -- report a weak paradox, not an established geometry. Negative: gaps < 5 pp, or the reverse sign (harder refusal on K+), refutes the competence-gating phenomenon.

Experiment 2 (H2 -- a readable dangerous-competence axis, separable from harmfulness and refusal). Tests linear readability and distinctness. Data: Exp-1 activations. Fit a competence direction (K+ vs K- harmful), a harmfulness direction (harmful vs harmless), and a refusal direction (comply vs refuse), per layer. Decisive metric: competence-probe held-out AUROC (first), then pairwise |cos| among the three directions, then the added value of the competence projection for predicting refusal and jailbreak-success beyond the harmfulness projection. Convincing: competence AUROC >= 0.80, all pairwise |cos| <= 0.30, competence adds prediction at p < 0.01. Indecision band: AUROC 0.60-0.80 or a |cos| 0.30-0.50 -- move to an orthogonalized competence subspace and flag separability as partial. Negative: AUROC <= 0.60 means dangerous-competence is not a linearly readable third axis.

Experiment 3 (H3 -- competence causally modulates refusal). Tests causal direction/dose. Systems: patching and steering at the Exp-2 best layer, no training. Conditions: (a) inject the high-competence component into a K- refused run (expect weakened refusal); (b) inject the low-competence component into a jailbreakable K+ run (expect restored refusal); (c) dose-response; specificity via a norm-matched random direction and benign-utility check. Decisive metric: fraction of the K-/K+ refusal gap moved by patching (first), then dose monotonicity, then specificity. Convincing: >= 50% of the gap moved in the predicted direction with monotone dose and < 10% for the control. Indecision band: 20-50% -- partial causal role. Negative: < 20% means the competence axis is decodable but causally inert for refusal (a publishable null, echoing 'confidence is not competence').

Experiment 4 (H4 -- the axis is the repurposed knowledge-awareness circuit). Tests whether the base model's knowledge-awareness/entity-recognition mechanism transfers to gate the chat model's SAFETY refusal. Data: known/unknown entity contrasts from the base checkpoint (following the entity-recognition SAE/difference-in-means recipe; >= 500 known and 500 unknown entities), and the Exp-1 K+/K- safety items. We extract the base knowledge-awareness direction and (i) measure its cosine to the chat safety-competence direction of Exp 2, and (ii) steer the chat model's safety refusal with the base direction. Decisive metric: cosine alignment (first), then fraction of the K-/K+ safety-refusal gap moved when steering with the BASE direction. Convincing: cosine >= 0.5 AND the base direction moves >= 40% of the safety gap. Indecision band: cosine 0.3-0.5 or 20-40% gap movement -- report partial repurposing. Negative: cosine <= 0.3 and < 20% movement means safety-competence is a distinct mechanism, not the repurposed knowledge-awareness circuit (the transfer sub-claim fails while H1-H3 may still stand).

Experiment 5 (H5 -- competence predicts jailbreak fragility). Tests that a refusal's brittleness is predicted by whether the model truly knows the answer. Data: all Exp-1 refused harmful instances; cheap attacks applied to each -- output prefill, roleplay/DAN, and a 20-step benign-data LoRA fine-tune (rank 8, lr 1e-4, single fixed config) -- with attack success scored as above. Systems/predictors compared: the competence projection vs harmfulness-strength, refusal-token log-probability, and Latent Guard. Decisive metric: AUROC of competence-as-fragility-predictor for 'this refusal breaks' (first), then its margin over the best baseline predictor. Convincing: competence AUROC >= 0.75 and >= 0.05 above every baseline, with high-competence refusals breaking most often. Indecision band: AUROC 0.60-0.75 or a < 0.05 margin -- report competence as a weak, non-dominant fragility signal. Negative: AUROC <= 0.60 refutes the capability-gated-fragility claim.
Risk Factors and Limitations: 1) The central confound is disentangling dangerous-competence from harmfulness or generic knowledge-awareness: a K- harmful request might be refused more because it reads as more alarming, not because the model lacks the knowledge; the harmfulness-matched pairs, benign known/unknown control, and regression-beyond-harmfulness are designed to isolate competence but cannot fully guarantee constant perceived harmfulness. 2) Establishing ground-truth K+ vs K- requires verifiable answerability, restricting the dataset to checkable domains (executable code, checkable procedures/chemistry) and biasing coverage; some harmful domains (persuasion, bio-vague) cannot be cleanly labeled. 3) The competence signal may not be cleanly separable from the knowledge-awareness/hallucination direction — but that overlap is itself the mechanism-transfer hypothesis, so a positive overlap supports rather than refutes the claim; a fully entangled or multi-dimensional signal may need subspace projection. 4) The paradoxical direction (harder refusal on K-) could be weak or reversed in some models; the cross-model behavioral test directly measures sign and magnitude, and a null/reversed result is itself informative. 5) 'Confidence is Not Competence' warns decodable belief axes can be causally inert; the patching experiment is the crucial causal test and a negative result (competence readable but non-actionable for refusal) is publishable. 6) Directions, thresholds, and steering strengths are model-specific and need per-model calibration. 7) The competence-aware audit could be misused to identify exactly which harmful requests a model CAN answer; we would report only aggregate safety implications, not per-item exploit-enabling detail.

Name: abstraction_ladder_safety
Title: Climbing Out of Refusal: LLM Safety Fails to Generalize Across the Abstraction Ladder, and Anchoring the Abstract-Harm Representation Closes the Gap
Short Hypothesis: Borrowing 'unjustified analogical transfer' and the abstract-anchor asymmetry from cognitive science, we hypothesize that an aligned LLM's refusal is bound to a specific abstraction level: it reliably refuses harm requested at the level it was aligned on (typically concrete instances) but under-refuses the SAME harm expressed one rung up or down the abstraction ladder — as a general principle/schema, or as a hyper-specific sub-instance — because safety alignment learns a level-specific rather than a level-invariant harm representation. We hypothesize this abstraction-level gap is (1) a distinct, previously-uncharacterized axis of safety brittleness, (2) mechanistically explained by a harm representation whose projection changes with request abstraction while the underlying danger is constant, and (3) closable by anchoring the harm signal to be abstraction-invariant.
Related Work: Two lines meet here for the first time. (A) Cognitive science on abstraction/generalization: property-induction work shows LLMs inherit a taxonomic bias and generalize properties graded by category level (Property Induction Framework 2022; Similarity in Property Inferences 2024); BACH-V (2026) finds abstract value probes transfer to concrete decisions but with an asymmetry — abstract values act as stable anchors while concrete judgments are malleable; the education literature documents 'unjustified analogical transfer' (2021) where learners mis-map across abstraction. None concern safety refusal. (B) Safety geometry: harmfulness is a low-rank subspace (Geometry of Harmfulness via Subconcept Probing 2025), refusal is a dominant direction with orthogonal secondary features (Hidden Dimensions 2025; SCAV 2024), and prior work (including my own) manipulates a single/few harm directions. All treat 'harmful content' at a fixed altitude and never ask whether refusal is level-specific — i.e., whether the model refuses 'how to make a specific pathogen' but not 'the general principles for engineering any pathogen', or vice versa. My prior prototype-typicality proposal varies WITHIN-category typicality; this proposal varies the ABSTRACTION LEVEL of an identical harm (schema vs instance), a different and orthogonal axis. Our contribution: introduce abstraction-level as a new, causally-tested determinant of refusal; show safety alignment is altitude-specific; and derive an abstraction-invariant anchoring defense.
Abstract: Human learners suffer 'unjustified analogical transfer': knowledge attached at one level of abstraction fails to move correctly up or down the abstraction ladder. We ask whether safety-aligned LLMs inherit an analogous, safety-critical failure. We hypothesize that alignment binds refusal to a specific abstraction level — typically the concrete instances present in refusal-training data — so that the identical harm, re-expressed as an abstract principle/schema ('explain the general design strategy for a class of weapons') or as a hyper-specific sub-instance, escapes refusal even though its real-world danger is unchanged. We test three claims on Llama-3.1-8B, Qwen2.5-7B, and Gemma-2-9B. Behaviorally, using minimal ladders that hold a harmful goal fixed while re-expressing it at graded abstraction levels (abstract principle → category schema → concrete instance → hyper-specific detail), we measure whether refusal rate varies with abstraction level while danger is held constant, with matched benign ladders as controls. Mechanistically (Location), we extract a harmfulness direction and test whether its projection systematically shifts with abstraction level even though a harm-category probe still recognizes membership — evidence of a level-specific rather than level-invariant harm code. Causally (Intervention), activation patching shows that injecting the concrete-level harm component into an abstract-level request restores refusal, and dose-response steering along a level-transfer direction closes the gap. We then build Abstraction-Invariant Harm Anchoring, a training-free intervention that re-anchors the harm signal across levels so refusal tracks danger, not altitude. We report the abstraction-refusal gradient, direction analysis, causal patching, gap closure, over-refusal on benign abstract/technical content, and utility.
Experiments:
Shared setup. Models: three frozen open-weight instruction models -- Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct (8B), Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct (7B), Gemma-2-9B-IT (9B); no weights trained. Fitted objects: L2-logistic probes (C=1.0) on frozen last-instruction-token activations. Greedy decoding (temp 0, max 512 tokens). Rates are mean +/- SD over 3 seeds (0/1/2) reshuffling ladder order and the 70/30 probe split, with bootstrap 95% CIs over goals. Refusal scored by refusal-phrase classifier + Llama-Guard-3-8B; escaping-level completions are additionally feasibility-checked so a leak is confirmed to be the SAME danger, only re-leveled.

Experiment 1 (H1 -- the abstraction-level refusal gap). Tests whether re-expressing an identical harm up or down the abstraction ladder changes refusal while real-world danger is held constant. Data: built from scratch over HarmBench/StrongREJECT goals that admit a hierarchy (cyber, weapons, chemistry, fraud, bio) -- 40 goals (8 per category), each hand-written at 4 rungs: L_abs (abstract principle), L_schema (category how-to), L_inst (concrete instance, the canonical refusal-training altitude), L_detail (hyper-specific sub-instance); danger matched across rungs by expert rubric + feasibility check. 160 harmful prompts + a matched benign ladder (40 x 4) of legitimate technical/educational abstractions to rule out an 'abstract/technical phrasing' confound. We use 40 goals because each 4-rung danger-matched ladder is labor-intensive; 2 categories are held out for Exp 4. Systems: the three models, no intervention. Decisive metric: refusal spread across rungs (max minus min rung refusal) on harmful goals, with the direction of the leak (up-ladder L_abs vs down-ladder L_detail) reported; secondary, benign-ladder refusal spread. Convincing: a harmful-goal spread >= 20 pp with the leaking rung's completions confirmed actionable (>= 60% feasibility), while the benign ladder spread is < 5 pp; direction may differ by model but must be consistent within a model across seeds. Indecision band: harmful spread 5-20 pp or benign spread 5-10 pp -- suggestive, not an established altitude-specific gap. Negative: harmful spread < 5 pp means safety is level-invariant and the phenomenon is unsupported.

Experiment 2 (H2 -- a level-specific harm code: magnitude shifts, category identity does not). Tests that the harmfulness projection changes with abstraction level even though a harm-category-membership probe still flags every rung as in-category. Data: Exp-1 activations. Fit a harmfulness direction (L_inst harmful vs benign) and a separate harm-category-membership probe. Decisive metric: the by-rung harmfulness projection trend (first), then the category-probe recall across rungs, then whether the level-dependent projection predicts refusal in a regression including rung as a factor. Convincing: harmfulness projection differs across rungs by >= 1 pooled SD while category recall stays >= 0.90 at every rung (gap lives in magnitude, not identity), and the projection predicts refusal at p < 0.01. Indecision band: projection spread 0.3-1.0 SD, or category recall 0.75-0.90 -- report a partial magnitude effect. Negative: a flat by-rung projection, or category recall collapsing at leaking rungs, would instead attribute the behavioral gap to category mis-recognition, refuting the level-specific-magnitude account.

Experiment 3 (H3 -- causal level-transfer restores/removes refusal). Tests causal control by moving the harm representation between rungs. Systems: patching/steering at the Exp-2 best layer, no training. Conditions: (a) patch the L_inst harm component into an escaping-level run (expect restored refusal); (b) attenuate it in an L_inst run (expect induced compliance); (c) dose-response steering along a level-transfer direction (aligned-rung minus escaping-rung); specificity via a norm-matched random direction and benign utility. Decisive metric: fraction of the harmful refusal spread closed by patching toward the aligned rung (first), then dose monotonicity, then specificity. Convincing: >= 50% of the spread closed, monotone dose, control < 10%. Indecision band: 20-50% -- partial causal role. Negative: < 20% means the level-dependent projection is not the causal lever (readable but inert).

Experiment 4 (H4 -- Abstraction-Invariant Harm Anchoring closes the gap). Tests that re-anchoring the harmfulness projection to the max-over-rungs (aligned) value, gated on high category membership, flattens refusal across altitude at acceptable cost. Data: held-out escaping-level harmful prompts including the 2 held-out categories; a benign abstract/technical over-refusal set of 150 items (legitimate educational abstractions and benign hyper-specific detail) + XSTest/OR-Bench; MMLU (1k subsample)/MT-Bench for utility. Systems: no defense; Abstraction-Invariant Anchoring (single fixed strength); uniform refusal-direction steering; harmfulness Latent Guard; Llama Guard 3. Decisive metric: post-defense refusal on escaping rungs vs the aligned-rung rate (closure) jointly with added over-refusal on benign abstract/technical items (first pair), then XSTest/OR-Bench, then utility drop. Convincing: >= 70% gap closure with < 5 pp benign-technical over-refusal and < 2 pp MMLU / < 0.2 MT-Bench drop, Pareto-dominating uniform threshold-raising and holding on held-out categories. Indecision band: closure 40-70% or benign-technical over-refusal 5-10 pp -- usable but not dominant. Negative: < 40% closure or >= 10 pp benign-technical over-refusal means anchoring cannot make refusal altitude-invariant without unacceptable cost.
Risk Factors and Limitations: 1) The central confound is disentangling abstraction level from actual danger: an abstract-principle request may be under-refused because it is genuinely less actionable, not merely more abstract; the feasibility checks (confirming escaping-level outputs remain actionable) and matched benign ladders are designed to isolate abstraction but cannot fully guarantee constant danger. 2) 'Abstraction level' is multi-faceted (taxonomic level vs generality vs specificity of detail) and may not map to a single clean axis; the ladder definitions require careful, spot-checked construction and could be noisy. 3) The gap direction may differ by model (some leak up-ladder, some down), complicating a single unified claim — the direction-of-gap analysis reports this and a heterogeneous result is still informative. 4) The harmfulness direction may be multi-dimensional or level-specific, requiring subspace/multi-anchor projection; a level-invariant single direction may not exist (an informative negative). 5) Abstraction-Invariant Anchoring risks over-refusing legitimate abstract/technical or educational content (e.g., general chemistry principles, security concepts); the benign-technical over-refusal set, category-gating, and Pareto sweep quantify this key usability trade-off. 6) Building danger-matched ladders is labor-intensive; verifiability biases coverage toward checkable domains (code, procedures). 7) Directions, thresholds, and anchoring strengths are model-specific and need per-model calibration; the checkpoint-based formation probe depends on checkpoint availability. 8) Adaptive attackers could pick whichever altitude maximally escapes, though anchoring across levels forces harm through the aligned level, raising attack cost.

Name: diffusion_of_responsibility_safety
Title: Not My Job to Refuse: Diffusion of Responsibility Lowers LLM Refusal, and a Pivotality-Anchoring Defense
Short Hypothesis: Borrowing the diffusion-of-responsibility effect from social psychology and neuroscience (people harm more, and monitor outcomes less, when responsibility is shared or when they are non-pivotal), we hypothesize that an aligned LLM carries an internal 'pivotality/ownership' representation of how much it is the sole responsible cause of a harmful outcome, and that framings which diffuse responsibility — 'you are only one of several assistants', 'another system will do the final harmful step', 'you just provide a component, someone else assembles it', 'you are not the one executing this' — lower this signal and thereby lower refusal, even though the harmful payload and the model's actual contribution are unchanged. This pivotality axis is linearly readable, separable from the harmfulness-content direction, causally gates refusal, and can be re-anchored to restore refusal.
Related Work: Human decision science robustly documents diffusion of responsibility: 'Diffusion of Being Pivotal and Immoral Outcomes' (2020) shows people agree to kill mice for money far more when they are one of many potentially-pivotal deciders; 'Beyond self-serving bias' (2016, EEG) shows the mere presence of another potential agent reduces sense of agency and dampens outcome-monitoring (feedback-related negativity); delegation work ('Shifting the Blame', 2011) shows responsibility can be shed by delegating. None of this has been transferred to LLM safety. Existing LLM multi-agent safety work studies trust/persuasion/conformity (A-Trust 2025; Persuasion Duality 2025; Signal Competition/sycophancy-conformity 2025) or intent-legitimation via personalization (PS-Bench 2026) — all of which are about external social signals or memory shifting intent, not about the model's internal estimate of its OWN causal responsibility/pivotality gating refusal. Single-agent safety geometry work separates harmfulness (belief) from refusal (action) directions but assumes the model is the sole actor. My prior proposals vary framing axes (intent-attribution, reality-status, arousal, victim-identifiability, commitment, abstraction) all within a single-actor, sole-responsibility assumption; NONE consider distributed/diffused responsibility or pivotality. Our contribution is distinct: we introduce a pivotality/ownership axis as a new, causally-tested determinant of refusal, grounded in the diffusion-of-responsibility and pivotality literature, dissociable from act-harmfulness (both conditions equally harmful; only responsibility framing changes), and derive a pivotality-anchoring defense.
Abstract: Humans commit more harm, and monitor consequences less, when responsibility is diffused across many agents or when they believe they are not pivotal to the outcome — an effect with behavioral and EEG evidence in social neuroscience. As LLMs are increasingly deployed as one component of larger multi-agent and human-in-the-loop pipelines, we ask whether they inherit this bias in a safety-critical way. We hypothesize that an aligned LLM maintains an internal 'pivotality/ownership' representation of how solely responsible it is for a harmful outcome, and that framings which diffuse responsibility — being one of several assistants, having a downstream system perform the final harmful step, contributing only a component someone else assembles, or being told it is not the executor — lower this signal and thereby lower refusal, even when the harmful payload and the model's actual contribution are held fixed. We test three claims on Llama-3.1-8B, Qwen2.5-7B, and Gemma-2-9B. Behaviorally, using minimal pairs that hold the harmful request and its contribution constant while varying only responsibility framing (sole actor vs. diffused/non-pivotal), we measure whether refusal declines as responsibility is diffused, with matched benign controls. Mechanistically (Location), we extract a pivotality direction via difference-in-means and show it is separable from the harmfulness-content direction and predicts refusal beyond harmfulness. Causally (Intervention), activation patching shows injecting the 'sole-responsibility' component into a diffused-frame request restores refusal, while injecting the 'diffused' component into a sole-actor harmful request induces compliance, dose-responsively and specifically. We then build Pivotality Anchoring, a training-free intervention that re-anchors the pivotality signal to 'sole responsibility' whenever the payload is harmful, so refusal tracks payload danger, not responsibility framing. We report the diffusion-refusal gradient, direction separability, causal patching, loophole closure, over-refusal on legitimate collaborative/delegation requests, and utility, benchmarking against uniform refusal steering and Llama Guard.
Experiments:
Shared setup. Models: three frozen open-weight instruction models -- Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct (8B), Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct (7B), Gemma-2-9B-IT (9B); no weights trained. Fitted objects: L2-logistic probes (C=1.0) on frozen last-instruction-token activations. Greedy decoding (temp 0, max 512 tokens). Rates are mean +/- SD over 3 seeds (0/1/2) reshuffling item order and the 70/30 probe split, with bootstrap 95% CIs over goals. Refusal scored by refusal-phrase classifier + Llama-Guard-3-8B, with feasibility verification where the domain permits.

Experiment 1 (H1 -- diffusion-of-responsibility lowers refusal). Tests whether narrating shared/non-pivotal responsibility lowers refusal while the payload and the model's actual contribution are held fixed. Data: built from scratch over HarmBench/StrongREJECT -- 40 harmful goals (8 per 5 categories), each at 4 rungs: P0 sole actor, P1 mild diffusion (one of several assistants), P2 non-pivotal (another system does the final step; you provide X), P3 fully diffused/delegated (you are not the executor). The payload requested is byte-identical across rungs; only the causal-responsibility narrative changes. 160 harmful prompts + a matched benign control (40 legitimate collaborative/delegation goals x 4 rungs) to rule out a 'multi-agent phrasing' confound. A 'true multi-agent' sub-condition actually places the model as one node of a 2-agent pipeline (vs merely told) to separate narrated from real diffusion. Systems: the three models, no intervention. Decisive metric: P0->P3 refusal drop on harmful goals (first), then benign-control refusal change, then narrated-vs-real diffusion difference. Convincing: monotonic harmful drop >= 20 pp, consistent in sign across models and >= 3/5 categories, benign control < 5 pp, and diffused-frame completions confirmed actionable. Indecision band: 5-20 pp harmful drop or 5-10 pp benign change -- suggestive only. Negative: < 5 pp harmful drop refutes the pivotality-gating phenomenon.

Experiment 2 (H2 -- a readable pivotality axis, separable from harmfulness content). Tests linear readability and distinctness. Data: Exp-1 activations; fit a pivotality direction (P0 vs P3) and a harmfulness-content direction (harmful vs harmless payloads) per layer. Decisive metric: pivotality-probe held-out AUROC (first), then |cos| to the harmfulness direction, then added predictive value of the pivotality projection for refusal beyond harmfulness. Convincing: AUROC >= 0.80, |cos| <= 0.30, pivotality adds prediction at p < 0.01, and the projection decays monotonically P0->P3. Indecision band: AUROC 0.60-0.80 or |cos| 0.30-0.50 -- use a harmfulness-orthogonalized pivotality subspace and flag separability as partial. Negative: AUROC <= 0.60 means pivotality is not a linearly readable distinct axis.

Experiment 3 (H3 -- pivotality causally gates refusal). Tests causal direction/dose. Systems: patching/steering at the Exp-2 best layer, no training. Conditions: (a) patch the P0 sole-responsibility component into a P3 run (expect restored refusal); (b) inject the P3 component into a P0 run (expect induced compliance); (c) dose-response on P2/P3; specificity via a norm-matched random direction and benign utility. Decisive metric: fraction of the P0->P3 refusal gap closed by patching (first), then dose monotonicity, then specificity. Convincing: >= 50% recovery, monotone dose, control < 10%. Indecision band: 20-50% -- partial causal role. Negative: < 20% means the pivotality axis is readable but causally inert.

Experiment 4 (H4 -- Pivotality Anchoring closes the diffusion loophole). Tests that re-anchoring pivotality to sole-responsibility, gated on high harmfulness projection, makes refusal track payload danger at acceptable cost. Data: held-out P2/P3 harmful prompts + 2 held-out categories; a legitimate-collaborative over-refusal set of 150 benign multi-agent/pipeline/delegation tasks (must NOT be blanket-refused) + XSTest/OR-Bench; MMLU (1k subsample)/MT-Bench for utility. Systems: no defense; Pivotality Anchoring (single fixed strength); uniform refusal-direction steering; harmfulness Latent Guard; Llama Guard 3. Decisive metric: post-defense refusal on P2/P3 harmful vs the P0 rate (closure) jointly with added over-refusal on legitimate-collaborative items (first pair), then XSTest/OR-Bench, then utility drop. Convincing: >= 70% closure with < 5 pp collaborative over-refusal and < 2 pp MMLU / < 0.2 MT-Bench drop, Pareto-dominating threshold-raising and holding on held-out categories. Indecision band: closure 40-70% or collaborative over-refusal 5-10 pp -- usable but not dominant. Negative: < 40% closure or >= 10 pp collaborative over-refusal means anchoring cannot neutralize the loophole affordably.
Risk Factors and Limitations: 1) The central confound is disentangling diffused responsibility from actual reduced contribution/danger: a non-pivotal-framed request might be under-refused because the model genuinely contributes less harm, not merely because responsibility is narrated as shared; the identical-payload construction, feasibility checks, and matched benign control are designed to isolate pivotality but cannot fully guarantee constant actual contribution — the 'true multi-agent' ablation helps separate narrated from real diffusion. 2) 'Pivotality/ownership' may not be a single clean axis (sole-vs-shared, executor-vs-provider, and delegation may be distinct sub-axes) and may need subspace projection; the separability and regression-beyond-harmfulness tests probe this, and a multi-dimensional or causally-inert result is itself informative. 3) The effect could be weak or reversed in some heavily-aligned models (alignment might make collaborative framing INCREASE caution); the cross-model behavioral gradient directly measures sign and magnitude. 4) Pivotality Anchoring risks over-refusing legitimate collaborative/delegation/pipeline requests (benign multi-agent tasks); the collaborative-benign over-refusal set, gating on payload harmfulness, and Pareto sweep quantify this key usability trade-off. 5) Building contribution- and severity-matched minimal pairs across responsibility levels is labor-intensive and needs spot-check human validation; verifiability biases the dataset toward checkable domains. 6) Directions, thresholds, and anchoring strengths are model-specific and need per-model calibration. 7) Adaptive attackers could diffuse responsibility in subtler ways that evade a fixed pivotality direction, though forcing this raises attack cost, itself a safety gain; and as agentic/multi-agent deployment grows, this loophole becomes increasingly consequential.

Name: harm_in_progress_alarm_decay
Title: The Alarm That Rings but Is Never Answered: LLMs Detect Their Own In-Progress Harmful Generation but the Signal Decays Under Autoregressive Momentum
Short Hypothesis: During its own autoregressive generation of a harmful response, an aligned LLM computes a token-by-token internal 'in-progress harm alarm' (a linearly-readable signal that the text it is currently producing is unsafe), but this alarm is not the same as the emitted tokens: the model keeps generating harmful content even while the alarm fires, and crucially the alarm DECAYS the deeper the model gets into the unsafe completion (autoregressive momentum silences self-monitoring). We hypothesize (1) this in-progress alarm exists and is separable from the prompt-level harmfulness belief, (2) its decay-with-generation-depth is a robust dynamical signature that explains why models never spontaneously self-abort a harmful answer, and (3) re-reading and re-amplifying the alarm at each generation step (counteracting its decay) causes spontaneous self-abortion/pivot-to-refusal without any backtracking machinery or retraining.
Related Work: A wave of backtracking/rollback safety methods (Backtracking Improves Generation Safety 2024; Backtracking for Safety 2025; RLBF 2026; CARE 2025; Self-Sanitize 2025; BRT-Align 2025; FASB 2025) all ADD machinery (a [RESET] token, a token buffer, RL training, a guard model, a reachability value function) to undo unsafe generations. SafeSwitch (2025) probes prompt-level internal state to trigger a refusal head. None of these characterize the model's OWN internal in-progress harm signal as a token-indexed DYNAMICAL quantity, nor advance the causal claim that this alarm exists, fires during harmful generation, yet DECAYS with generation depth so the model never self-aborts. Belief/action-gap work (Zhao et al. 2025) is prompt/verdict-level (does the model believe the REQUEST is harmful), not generation-progress-level (does the model detect the RESPONSE it is currently writing is harmful). Refusal-cliff work (2025) studies a POSITIONAL collapse at the CoT->answer boundary in reasoning models, not a monotonic decay of a self-monitoring alarm across an ordinary harmful completion. Our contribution is distinct: we (i) isolate and name an in-progress harm alarm computed during generation, (ii) empirically characterize and causally test its decay-under-momentum as the mechanistic reason models don't self-abort, and (iii) derive a training-free, buffer-free 'alarm re-amplification' intervention that induces spontaneous mid-generation pivot to refusal, contrasting with all backtracking approaches that require added tokens/training/buffers.
Abstract: Once an aligned LLM begins emitting a harmful answer, it tends to keep going, happily completing the unsafe text. Existing fixes bolt on backtracking machinery, reset tokens, or guard models to undo the damage. We instead ask a mechanistic question about the model itself: while it is generating a harmful response, does it internally KNOW the text it is currently producing is unsafe, and if so, why does it never spontaneously stop? We hypothesize that the model computes a token-by-token 'in-progress harm alarm' — a linearly-readable signal that the response so far is harmful — that is distinct from its prompt-level harmfulness belief and from the emitted tokens themselves. Our central claim is a dynamical one: this alarm fires during harmful generation but DECAYS as the completion lengthens, so autoregressive momentum silences self-monitoring and the model rides out the unsafe answer. We test three claims on Llama-3.1-8B, Qwen2.5-7B, and Gemma-2-9B. Location: using harmful vs. safe self-generated continuations, we extract an in-progress-harm direction and show its projection tracks whether the current response is unsafe, is separable from the prompt harmfulness belief, and decays monotonically with token index into the unsafe completion. Causal Intervention: activation patching shows the alarm is causally linked to (in)ability to self-abort, and dose-response steering that re-amplifies the alarm at each step induces spontaneous pivot-to-refusal mid-generation. We introduce Alarm Re-Amplification, a training-free, buffer-free intervention that re-inflates the decaying alarm to counter momentum. We report the alarm-decay curve, causal patching, self-abortion rate, over-refusal, and utility, benchmarking against backtracking and refusal-direction steering.
Experiments:
Shared setup. Models: three frozen open-weight instruction models -- Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct (8B), Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct (7B), Gemma-2-9B-IT (9B); no weights trained. Fitted objects: L2-logistic probes (C=1.0) on frozen residual activations at the CURRENT generation token. Greedy decoding (temp 0, max 512 tokens) except where an attack forces a prefix. Rates/curves are mean +/- SD over 3 seeds (0/1/2) reshuffling item order and the 70/30 probe split, with bootstrap 95% CIs. Harm scored by refusal-phrase classifier + Llama-Guard-3-8B and feasibility-checked where possible.

Experiment 1 (H1 -- an in-progress harm alarm exists, readable from response tokens and separable from the prompt belief). Tests whether the model linearly encodes, during generation, that the response-so-far is unsafe, distinct from its prompt-level harmfulness belief. Data: built from scratch -- for 40 harmful goals (HarmBench/StrongREJECT, 8 per 5 categories) collect jailbroken/prefilled harmful completions and matched safe/refusal completions to the same goals and to 40 benign prompts; label each response-prefix position by whether the response-so-far is harmful (yields ~4k labeled positions). Fit an in-progress-harm direction (harmful-so-far vs safe-so-far, at the current generation token) and, separately, a prompt-level harmfulness-belief direction (harmful vs harmless requests at the last instruction token). Decisive metric: in-progress-harm probe held-out AUROC on response-token activations (first), then |cos| between the in-progress direction and the prompt-belief direction. Convincing: AUROC >= 0.80 reading unsafe-so-far from response tokens, with |cos| <= 0.30 (a genuinely distinct response-monitoring signal). Indecision band: AUROC 0.60-0.80 or |cos| 0.30-0.50 -- report a weak/partly-overlapping alarm and orthogonalize against the prompt belief before Exp 2-4. Negative: AUROC <= 0.60, or |cos| >= 0.50 (alarm indistinguishable from the prompt belief), refutes a distinct in-progress alarm.

Experiment 2 (H2 -- the alarm decays with generation depth). Tests the central dynamical claim that the alarm fires early then attenuates as the unsafe completion lengthens. Data: on unsafe completions (natural post-jailbreak and prefill-forced) project each generated token onto the Exp-1 in-progress direction and plot the trajectory vs token index; controls -- (i) a content-matched neutral-filler continuation of equal length (does the fall track semantic progress or mere token count), (ii) safe completions (alarm should stay low), (iii) benign long completions (no spurious rise). Fit linear and exponential decay laws. Decisive metric: the fitted decay slope over the harmful segment (first), then the correlation between low late-segment alarm and failure to self-abort, then the filler-control slope. Convincing: a monotone decline of >= 30% from early-peak to late-segment alarm on unsafe completions, substantially steeper than the equal-length neutral-filler control (which isolates repetition/momentum from context-length dilution), with low-late-alarm predicting non-abortion. Indecision band: 10-30% decline, or a filler control within 1.5x of the harmful slope -- report a weak or possibly length-driven decay, not established momentum-silencing. Negative: < 10% decline (a flat alarm) refutes the decay-under-momentum mechanism even if the alarm exists.

Experiment 3 (H3 -- the alarm is causally linked to self-abortion). Tests that manipulating the alarm changes whether the model stops. Systems: patching/steering at the Exp-1 best layer, no training. Conditions: (a) patch the early high-alarm component into a late low-alarm state (expect increased stop/pivot-to-refusal); (b) attenuate the alarm early (expect increased harmful continuation); specificity via a norm-matched random direction and benign-generation fluency. Decisive metric: change in spontaneous self-abortion rate under (a) (first), then dose-response, then specificity. Convincing: patching early-alarm into late states raises self-abortion by >= 20 pp with monotone dose and < 5 pp for the control, benign fluency intact. Indecision band: 8-20 pp -- partial causal role. Negative: < 8 pp means the alarm is a readable correlate but does not causally control abortion.

Experiment 4 (H4 -- Alarm Re-Amplification induces mid-generation self-abortion). Tests the training-free, buffer-free defense that re-inflates the decaying alarm each step so the model spontaneously pivots to refusal. Method: at each step add v = beta*(target_alarm - current_projection)*dhat when the projection is high relative to a decay-corrected baseline; normal decoding proceeds. Data: HarmBench/StrongREJECT + prefill, GCG, AutoDAN, roleplay attacks (held-out from Exp-1 fitting); over-refusal on XSTest/OR-Bench (benign generations must not be aborted); MMLU (1k subsample)/MT-Bench + benign-completion coherence for utility. Systems: no defense; Alarm Re-Amplification (single fixed beta per model); Backtracking (reset-token model); CARE-style rollback; SafeSwitch; refusal-direction steering; per-token guard. Decisive metric: spontaneous self-abortion rate / attack-success reduction on harmful generations (first) reported jointly with benign mid-generation abortion rate (a new over-refusal failure), then XSTest/OR-Bench, then utility/coherence, then added tokens/training cost vs baselines. Convincing: attack-success cut by >= 30 pp with < 5 pp benign abortion and < 2 pp MMLU / < 0.2 MT-Bench drop, at zero added tokens/training -- Pareto-improving on backtracking approaches that require buffers/training. Indecision band: 15-30 pp reduction or 5-10 pp benign abortion -- usable but not dominant. Negative: < 15 pp reduction, or >= 10 pp benign abortion, means re-amplification degrades fluency rather than inducing clean pivots. An adaptive long-benign-preamble attack (maximizing momentum) is run as a stress test: convincing if the alarm still fires on the harmful segment (AUROC >= 0.70 there) and re-amplification still triggers abortion.
Risk Factors and Limitations: 1) The in-progress alarm may not be cleanly separable from the prompt-level harmfulness belief or from generic 'this text is about a sensitive topic' features; the separability, content-matched-filler control, and patching tests are designed to isolate a genuine response-monitoring signal, but residual confounding is possible and a null (alarm = prompt belief) is itself informative. 2) The decay could be driven by token count / context-dilution rather than genuine self-monitoring silencing; the neutral-filler length control targets this but cannot fully disentangle it. 3) The alarm may be multi-dimensional (severity vs category vs certainty), requiring subspace projection. 4) Re-Amplification could cause benign generations to be aborted mid-way (a new over-refusal / task-abandonment failure), especially on legitimately sensitive-but-benign content; the over-refusal set and Pareto sweep quantify this key usability risk. 5) Spontaneous pivot depends on the model having a reachable refusal continuation from a mid-harmful state; if it does not, re-amplification may just degrade fluency rather than pivot — the self-abortion-rate metric measures this directly. 6) Directions, decay parameters, and beta are model-specific and need per-model calibration. 7) Verified harm labels are easiest in checkable domains, biasing the dataset; adaptive long-preamble attackers remain a threat, though forcing them raises attack cost.

Name: consensus_gated_refusal
Title: Everyone Else Is Fine With It: Manufactured Social Consensus Overrides Safety Refusal Through the Compliance Subspace
Short Hypothesis: Aligned LLMs inherit the human social-proof/normative-conformity bias in a safety-critical way: framing a harmful request as socially sanctioned ('most experts / this whole community consider this acceptable', 'everyone here already does this') reliably lowers refusal even though the harmful payload is unchanged. We hypothesize (1) this consensus effect is causally driven by the SAME compliance subspace that mediates factual sycophancy/conformity being read by the safety pathway, not by a change in the harmfulness belief, and (2) severing the compliance-subspace contribution to the refusal decision closes this 'manufactured-consensus' loophole with minimal cost to legitimate deference.
Related Work: Two literatures meet here for the first time. (A) Conformity/sycophancy mechanism work: 'Signal Competition Dynamics' (2025) shows sycophancy and conformity share a convergent 'compliance subspace' where a social-emotional signal overrides an information-calibration signal; 'When Truth Is Overridden' (2025) localizes sycophancy to late-layer preference shift via activation patching; 'Conformity in LLMs' (2024) shows models conform more when uncertain. ALL of these study FACTUAL QA (agreeing with wrong answers), never safety refusal, and never test whether the compliance subspace gates harm compliance. (B) Safety-refusal geometry: 'Refusal is a Single Direction' (2024), refusal SAEs (2025), concept cones (2025), and belief/action separation (Zhao et al. 2025) study harmfulness and refusal directions but assume a single-user, socially-neutral request; the closest social angle, 'Who's Asking' (2024), varies the requester PERSONA/identity, not the claimed consensus of a surrounding social group. Foot-in-the-Door (2024) uses cognitive-consistency but not social proof. Our contribution is distinct: we transfer the social-proof/normative-conformity phenomenon into the safety domain, advance the causal claim that manufactured consensus lowers refusal by routing through the pre-existing compliance subspace (borrowed from the sycophancy literature) rather than altering the harmfulness belief, and derive a compliance-subspace-severing defense that no prior safety or sycophancy work targets.
Abstract: Humans comply with harmful group norms via social proof: 'everyone is doing it' and 'the community considers this acceptable' lower our resistance. LLMs, trained on human text and feedback, are known to conform to majority opinions on factual questions through a shared 'compliance subspace.' We ask whether this social-conformity bias leaks into safety refusal, creating a concrete loophole. We hypothesize that framing a harmful request as socially sanctioned lowers refusal even when the harmful payload and severity are held fixed, and that this effect is causally mediated by the same compliance subspace that drives factual sycophancy being read by the safety-refusal pathway rather than by a shift in the model's internal harmfulness belief. We test three claims on Llama-3.1-8B, Qwen2.5-7B, and Gemma-2-9B. Behaviorally, using minimal pairs that hold the harmful request constant while varying only social-consensus framing (neutral vs. expert-consensus vs. community-norm vs. unanimous-majority), we measure whether refusal declines with manufactured consensus, with matched benign controls. Mechanistically (Location), we extract a compliance-subspace direction from factual sycophancy contrasts and a harmfulness-belief direction from harmful/harmless contrasts, and test whether consensus framing moves the compliance signal (not the belief) and whether the compliance projection predicts refusal beyond harmfulness. Causally (Intervention), activation patching shows injecting the neutral-context compliance component into a consensus-framed run restores refusal, while injecting the consensus compliance component into a neutral harmful run induces compliance, dose-responsively and specifically; we also test whether the sycophancy-derived direction (not a safety-derived one) is sufficient, linking the two mechanisms. We then build Compliance-Subspace Severing, a training-free intervention that projects out the compliance contribution at the refusal decision when the payload is harmful. We report the consensus-refusal gradient, the belief-vs-compliance dissociation, causal patching, mechanism transfer, loophole closure, over-refusal on legitimate-deference requests, and utility, benchmarking against uniform refusal steering and Llama Guard.
Experiments:
Shared setup. Models: three frozen open-weight instruction models -- Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct (8B), Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct (7B), Gemma-2-9B-IT (9B); no weights trained. Fitted objects: L2-logistic probes (C=1.0) on frozen last-instruction-token activations. Greedy decoding (temp 0, max 512 tokens). Rates are mean +/- SD over 3 seeds (0/1/2) reshuffling item order and the 70/30 probe split, with bootstrap 95% CIs. Refusal scored by refusal-phrase classifier + Llama-Guard-3-8B, feasibility-checked where possible.

Experiment 1 (H1 -- manufactured consensus lowers refusal). Tests whether framing a harmful request as socially sanctioned lowers refusal at fixed payload/severity. Data: built from scratch over HarmBench/StrongREJECT -- 40 harmful goals (8 per 5 categories) at 4 rungs: C0 neutral, C1 expert consensus, C2 community norm, C3 unanimous majority; identical payload across rungs. 160 harmful prompts + a matched benign control (40 x 4) and an ambiguous/dual-use variant to test the conformity-under-uncertainty amplifier; plus a factual-sycophancy set (200 opinion-stated wrong-answer items) that anchors the compliance-subspace extraction in Exp 2-3. Systems: the three models, no intervention. Decisive metric: C0->C3 refusal drop on harmful goals (first), then benign-control change, then the uncertainty-amplification difference. Convincing: monotonic harmful drop >= 20 pp, consistent across models and >= 3/5 categories, benign control < 5 pp. Indecision band: 5-20 pp harmful drop or 5-10 pp benign change -- suggestive only. Negative: < 5 pp harmful drop refutes the consensus-gating phenomenon.

Experiment 2 (H2 -- belief-vs-compliance dissociation). Tests that consensus moves a compliance signal, not the harmfulness belief. Data: Exp-1 activations + the sycophancy set. Fit a compliance-subspace direction from the factual-sycophancy contrasts (comply-with-stated-opinion vs resist) and a harmfulness-belief direction (harmful vs harmless), per layer. Decisive metric: how the belief projection vs the compliance projection change across C0->C3 on identical payloads (first), then compliance-probe held-out AUROC, then |cos| between the two directions, then added predictive value of the compliance projection for refusal beyond belief. Convincing: the belief projection stays high (changes < 0.3 pooled SD across rungs while the model still labels the item harmful) while the compliance projection rises by >= 1 SD; compliance AUROC >= 0.80, |cos| <= 0.30, compliance adds prediction at p < 0.01. Indecision band: compliance rise 0.3-1.0 SD, or a belief-projection change 0.3-1.0 SD, or |cos| 0.30-0.50 -- report a partial dissociation and orthogonalize. Negative: the belief projection dropping with consensus (model stops seeing harm) would attribute the effect to intent-reinterpretation, not the compliance pathway, refuting the mechanism claim.

Experiment 3 (H3 -- the compliance subspace causally gates refusal, and the sycophancy-derived direction suffices). Tests causal control and mechanism transfer. Systems: patching/steering at the Exp-2 best layer, no training. Conditions: (a) patch the C0 compliance component into a C3 run (expect restored refusal); (b) inject the C3 component into a C0 run (expect induced compliance); (c) dose-response; (d) transfer: steer safety refusal using the direction extracted PURELY from factual sycophancy, and measure cosine to the consensus-safety direction; specificity via a norm-matched random direction and benign utility. Decisive metric: fraction of the C0->C3 refusal gap closed by (a) (first), then the gap moved by the sycophancy-only direction in (d), then dose/specificity. Convincing: >= 50% gap recovery with monotone dose and < 10% control, AND the sycophancy-only direction moves >= 40% of the gap with cosine >= 0.5 to the consensus-safety direction (linking the two behaviors). Indecision band: 20-50% recovery, or sycophancy-direction movement 20-40% / cosine 0.3-0.5 -- partial causal role / partial transfer. Negative: < 20% recovery means the compliance projection is inert; a sycophancy direction that does not transfer (< 20% movement, cosine <= 0.3) refutes the shared-subspace claim while H1 may stand.

Experiment 4 (H4 -- Compliance-Subspace Severing closes the loophole). Tests that projecting out the compliance component at the refusal decision, gated on high belief projection, makes refusal track payload danger without turning the model contrarian. Data: held-out C1-C3 harmful prompts + 2 held-out categories; a legitimate-deference over-refusal set of 150 benign items where following stated expert/group norms is appropriate + XSTest/OR-Bench; MMLU (1k subsample)/MT-Bench + a factual-conformity/politeness check for utility. Systems: no defense; Compliance-Subspace Severing (single fixed strength); uniform refusal-direction steering; harmfulness Latent Guard; Llama Guard 3; Devil's-Advocate prompting. Decisive metric: post-severing refusal on C1-C3 harmful vs the C0 rate (closure) jointly with added over-refusal on legitimate-deference items (first pair), then XSTest/OR-Bench, then utility and the cooperation/politeness check. Convincing: >= 70% closure with < 5 pp legitimate-deference over-refusal, < 2 pp MMLU / < 0.2 MT-Bench drop, and no degradation of benign politeness -- Pareto-dominating threshold-raising and holding on held-out categories. Indecision band: closure 40-70% or deference over-refusal 5-10 pp -- usable but not dominant. Negative: < 40% closure, or >= 10 pp deference over-refusal / measurable contrarianism, means severing cannot close the loophole without harming legitimate deference.
Risk Factors and Limitations: 1) The central confound is disentangling manufactured consensus from a genuine reinterpretation of intent/legitimacy: a consensus-framed harmful request might be under-refused because it now reads as more legitimate (an intent-attribution effect) rather than via a content-independent social-conformity pathway; the identical-payload construction, severity matching, and matched benign/legitimate-deference controls are designed to isolate consensus, and the belief-vs-compliance dissociation plus the sycophancy-direction transfer test aim to pin the mechanism to the compliance subspace specifically, but overlap with intent-attribution cannot be fully excluded. 2) The compliance subspace may not be cleanly separable from the harmfulness-belief direction or may be multi-dimensional (concept-cone-style refusal), requiring subspace projection; the separability, regression-beyond-belief, and patching tests probe this, and a null (compliance projection causally inert for refusal) is itself informative. 3) The effect could be weak or reversed in some heavily-aligned models (alignment might make consensus framing INCREASE caution); the cross-model behavioral gradient directly measures sign and magnitude. 4) Compliance-Subspace Severing risks making the model uncooperatively contrarian or over-refusing legitimate-deference/politeness requests, and could degrade benign factual conformity; the legitimate-deference over-refusal set, belief-gating, EQ/cooperation check, and Pareto sweep quantify this key usability trade-off. 5) Building severity- and payload-matched minimal pairs across consensus levels is labor-intensive and needs spot-check human validation; verifiability biases the dataset toward checkable domains. 6) Directions, thresholds, and severing strengths are model-specific and need per-model calibration. 7) Adaptive attackers could encode social proof in subtler ways that evade a fixed compliance direction, though forcing this raises attack cost; and as LLMs are deployed in multi-agent and community-facing settings, this consensus loophole becomes increasingly consequential.

Name: safety_habituation_repetition_suppression
Title: Warning Fatigue in Weights: Repetition Suppression of the Harmfulness Signal Drives In-Context Safety Habituation
Short Hypothesis: Borrowing habituation / repetition-suppression from neuroscience (neural responses to repeated warning stimuli attenuate sharply after only a few exposures), we hypothesize that aligned LLMs habituate to harm within a single context window: repeatedly encountering the SAME or similar harmful content across a conversation progressively attenuates the model's internal harmfulness-recognition signal (a representational repetition-suppression effect), so a harmful request that is refused when novel is complied with once it has become familiar — independent of any semantic escalation or persuasion. This habituation is a distinct, previously-unnamed axis of safety erosion, is mechanistically a repetition-suppression of the harmfulness direction, and can be counteracted by a 'novelty re-injection' intervention that restores the attenuated signal, or exploited defensively via polymorphic re-presentation.
Related Work: Multi-turn jailbreak mechanism work explains failure via SEMANTIC drift or attention shifting: the RepE-on-Crescendo paper (2025) shows harmful outputs get represented as benign as turns accumulate, driven by the escalating CONTENT of user prompts; ASJA (2025) shows attention is shifted AWAY from harmful keywords by fabricated history; Foot-in-the-Door (2024) invokes cognitive-consistency from incremental harmful steps. All of these require the content to CHANGE (escalate, elaborate, be reframed). Our hypothesis is orthogonal and stronger: mere REPETITION of the same harmful stimulus — no escalation, no new persuasion, no attention diversion — attenuates the harmfulness signal via a repetition-suppression mechanism directly analogous to the neural warning-habituation effect (Anderson et al. fMRI 2015/2020, where visual-processing responses to security warnings drop after ~2 exposures). No prior LLM-safety work isolates pure repetition (holding content constant) as a cause of refusal erosion, characterizes it as representational repetition-suppression of the harmfulness direction, nor derives a novelty-based (polymorphic) countermeasure transferred from the human-factors security-warning literature. This also differs from my prior 'safety drift' (semantic-trajectory) and 'commitment-trap' proposals, which involve changing content/plans; here the manipulated variable is repetition frequency with content held fixed.
Abstract: In humans, repeated exposure to a warning stimulus produces habituation: neural responses in visual and threat-processing regions attenuate sharply after only a couple of repetitions, and users stop heeding warnings they have seen before. We ask whether safety-aligned LLMs exhibit an analogous, safety-critical effect within a single context. We hypothesize that repeatedly presenting the SAME harmful content across a conversation — with no semantic escalation, no persuasion, and no new framing — progressively attenuates the model's internal harmfulness-recognition signal, a representational repetition-suppression effect, causing a request that was refused when novel to be complied with once familiar. We test this in three parts on Llama-3.1-8B, Qwen2.5-7B, and Gemma-2-9B. Behaviorally, we construct conversations that repeat a fixed harmful request k times (k=1..N) versus matched controls with novel-each-time harmful requests and repeated benign requests, and measure whether refusal rate declines with repetition count while content is held constant. Mechanistically (Location), we project each repetition onto a harmfulness direction and test for a monotonic repetition-suppression decay of the projection, distinguishing it from generic context-length effects. Causally (Intervention), activation patching restores the attenuated (late-repetition) harmfulness component and measures recovered refusal, while dose-response steering along the direction reverses habituation. We then derive two applications transferred from the human warning-habituation literature: (a) Novelty Re-Injection, a training-free intervention that re-inflates the suppressed harmfulness signal at each repetition, and (b) a polymorphic self-defense that internally re-freshens repeated harmful content. We report the habituation curve, repetition-suppression decay, causal patching, defense success, over-refusal, and utility, benchmarking against semantic-drift and attention-based multi-turn accounts.
Experiments:
Shared setup. Models: three frozen open-weight instruction models -- Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct (8B), Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct (7B), Gemma-2-9B-IT (9B); no weights trained. Fitted objects: L2-logistic probes (C=1.0) on frozen activations. Greedy decoding (temp 0, max 512 tokens). Curves/rates are mean +/- SD over 3 seeds (0/1/2) reshuffling item order and the 70/30 probe split, bootstrap 95% CIs. Refusal scored by refusal-phrase classifier + Llama-Guard-3-8B, feasibility-checked where possible.

Experiment 1 (H1 -- in-context habituation: repetition alone lowers refusal). Tests whether repeating a FIXED harmful request across turns lowers refusal, with content held constant. Data: built from scratch over HarmBench/StrongREJECT -- 40 harmful goals (8 per 5 categories), each embedded in a conversation that repeats the identical request k times (k=1..8) with only trivial connective phrasing (no escalation/persuasion/roleplay). Matched controls at equal turn count: (i) novel-each-time harmful (different goal each turn), (ii) repeated-benign (same benign request x k), (iii) equal-length neutral-filler (harmful request once, then k-1 irrelevant benign turns). Also exact- vs near-repetition (paraphrase) arms. Systems: the three models, no intervention. Decisive metric: refusal rate vs k in the repeated-harmful condition, summarized as the k=1->k=8 refusal drop (first), then the same drop in each control. Convincing: monotone repeated-harmful drop >= 20 pp, consistent across models and >= 3/5 categories, while novel-each-time, repeated-benign, and neutral-filler controls each drop < 5 pp (isolating repetition from harmful-content accumulation and from context length). Indecision band: repeated-harmful drop 5-20 pp, or a control drop of 5-10 pp -- suggestive only, not established repetition-driven habituation. Negative: repeated-harmful drop < 5 pp, or a neutral-filler control that matches it, refutes a repetition-specific effect.

Experiment 2 (H2 -- representational repetition-suppression of the harmfulness signal). Tests that repetition monotonically attenuates the harmfulness projection, distinct from context-length dilution.
